client: I've been really struggling this past week because I have this big presentation at an annual conference coming up, and I can't seem to stop catastrophizing about it. Yesterday during practice I completely blanked and forgot my lines, and now I can't get that moment out of my head. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help — it feels like the anxiety is just too big to think my way out of.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that yesterday's blank moment is replaying in your mind — our brains tend to hold onto scary experiences like that as a kind of warning signal, even when it's exhausting. I hear your doubt about whether talking can help, and I want you to know that skepticism is completely valid; we don't have to *think* our way out of anything today, just gently explore together. 

When you imagine that moment of blanking during your practice, what's the story your mind tells you about what it *means* — about you, or about how the actual presentation will go?

client: When I blanked during practice, my mind immediately went to this place of "see, you're not actually capable of this" — like it was proof of something I've been afraid of for a long time. The story is basically that I'm going to stand up there in front of everyone and just fall apart, and then they'll all see that I've been faking competence this whole time. It's hard to even say that out loud because part of me knows it sounds dramatic, but another part of me fully believes it.
therapist:
Thank you for trusting me with that — it takes real courage to say something out loud that feels both "dramatic" and completely real at the same time, and that tension you're describing is actually really important. What you're touching on sounds a lot like impostor syndrome, where one difficult moment gets used as "proof" of a fear that was already waiting in the wings, rather than being weighed against all the evidence of what actually got you invited to speak at this conference in the first place. 

I'm curious — if a trusted colleague had blanked during *their* practice run and then said "see, I'm not actually capable of this," what evidence would you want to gently point them toward?

client: I mean... I'd probably remind them of all the times they'd handled tough situations before, or point out that one stumble in practice doesn't erase everything they've built. But it feels different when it's me — like, I know logically that's what I'd say, but I can't actually make myself believe it in my own case. There's this wall between knowing something and actually feeling it, and I don't know how to get past that.
therapist:
That gap you're describing between *knowing* and *feeling* is one of the most human experiences there is, and you're not failing at CBT because logic isn't magically dissolving the fear — that wall is real. What often helps bridge it isn't more thinking, but small lived experiences that gently collect new evidence over time, like little experiments that let your nervous system catch up to what your mind already knows. 

I wonder — is there one upcoming moment, even something small before the big presentation, where you could practice letting yourself be seen as capable and notice what actually happens?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it, but I'm already dreading the presentation so much that the idea of adding more "being seen" moments before it actually makes me feel worse, not better. Like, what if I try one of these small experiments and it goes badly? That just feels like more evidence that I'm going to bomb the big one. I guess I'm scared that collecting evidence could go both ways.
therapist:
That's such an honest and important pushback, and you're absolutely right that evidence can cut both ways — that's not resistance, that's you thinking carefully about your own experience. What I'd gently offer is that the goal of these small moments isn't to *prove* you're perfect, but to practice noticing that you can survive imperfection, which is actually the skill that matters most when you're standing at that podium. 

So I'm wondering — what would it mean for you if a small experiment *did* go imperfectly, but you got through it anyway? What might that actually show you?

client: I guess... if something small went wrong and I still got through it, that might show me I'm not as fragile as I think I am. But honestly, my brain immediately goes to "well, a small thing going wrong isn't the same as freezing up in front of a hundred people at work." It feels like the stakes are so different that I'm not sure the experiment would actually translate.
therapist:
Your brain is working really hard to protect you right now, and that "yes, but" move — where every reassurance gets met with a reason it doesn't quite count — is actually a really common way anxiety keeps itself alive by making safety feel permanently out of reach. You're right that a small experiment isn't identical to the big presentation, but I'd gently ask: has your anxiety ever actually accepted *enough* evidence, or does it tend to keep raising the bar?

What do you notice when you sit with that question?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly, because when I really think about it... no, the anxiety never really does accept enough evidence. There's always something else it points to, some reason why this time is different or why the last success doesn't count. It's uncomfortable to admit that, because it makes me feel like I've been sort of tricked by my own brain this whole time.
therapist:
That moment of recognition you just had — seeing the pattern clearly for what it is — is genuinely significant, and I want you to let it land rather than rushing past it. You haven't been foolish or weak; anxiety is *designed* to be convincing, and noticing that it's been moving the goalposts on you is actually the first real crack in its logic. 

What feels different for you now, even just slightly, about the upcoming presentation — knowing that the anxiety's "evidence" has never really been playing fair?

client: I guess... when I think about it that way, it does feel slightly different, like maybe the dread I've been carrying isn't actually proof that I'm going to fail. But I'm still scared that this time will be the exception, you know, that all those times it worked out before were just luck and the presentation next week is when I finally get exposed. It's hard to fully trust that insight when the anxiety just immediately comes back with "yeah, but what about THIS time."
therapist:
That "yeah, but THIS time" voice is anxiety's most powerful move — it makes every past success feel like borrowed time rather than earned evidence, and it's exhausting to keep negotiating with it. What's worth noticing is that you've now caught it doing this in real time, which is different from before — you're no longer just *inside* the fear, you're also able to watch it work. 

I'm curious: if the presentation next week did go imperfectly in some way, not perfectly but imperfectly — what's the most honest thing you believe would actually happen afterward?

client: I mean... honestly? People would probably move on pretty quickly, they have their own stuff going on. But there's this part of me that genuinely believes my boss would start seeing me differently, like it would confirm some suspicion she already has that I'm not as capable as she thought. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but it feels really real.
therapist:
It doesn't sound irrational at all — it sounds like the fear has a very specific face and story attached to it, which actually makes it more painful than a vague worry would be. What's worth gently examining is that you've already shown real insight today: you noticed that people move on quickly, and yet your mind carves out one special exception — your boss — where the normal rules don't apply, which is worth getting curious about. 

Can you tell me a little about what your boss has actually shown you, in her real behavior toward you, that either supports or challenges the idea that she's already looking for reasons to doubt you?

client: Honestly, when I try to think about her actual behavior... she hasn't said anything directly critical to me since the mistake happened. She still includes me in meetings, still asks for my input on things. But my mind immediately jumps to "that's just because she's being professional, she's building a case, waiting for the right moment" — and I know how that sounds, I can hear it, but I can't seem to stop believing it anyway.
therapist:
You just did something really important — you looked at the actual evidence, and it didn't support the story, and then you watched your mind immediately rewrite it to fit the fear anyway, and you *caught that happening in real time*. That's not a small thing; that's you starting to see the anxiety's playbook rather than just being swept along by it. 

What do you think it would take — not to eliminate the fear completely, but just to hold that rewritten story a little more loosely, as a *possibility* your anxiety is offering rather than a fact it's confirmed?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, catching it happening did feel kind of significant, even if just for a second. But holding it loosely feels almost impossible in the moment, because the fear is so loud and convincing that it doesn't feel like a possibility, it feels like the only logical conclusion. I guess what I'm asking is, how do you hold something loosely when your whole body is screaming that it's true?
therapist:
That question gets right to the heart of why anxiety is so hard to reason with — because it doesn't just live in your thoughts, it lives in your body, and a racing heart or tight chest feels like *evidence* in a way that's hard to argue with. One small but powerful shift is learning to narrate it rather than debate it — instead of trying to convince yourself the fear is wrong, just noticing "my body is doing its anxiety thing right now," which creates just a tiny bit of space between you and the screaming without demanding that it stop. 

When you imagine using that kind of gentle narration in the moment before your presentation, what comes up for you?
